summaries.summary: Word embeddings are numerical vectors from neural learning tasks such as word2vec, GloVe, FastText, ELMo, and BERT, trained on large monolingual corpora to preserve semantic relations.
word2vec fails to express polysemous words because all senses contribute by frequency, poorly representing rare meanings, as with paper and its 50 closest vectors.
Contextual embeddings generate sentence-wise vectors, and this work describes high-quality ELMo models for seven morphologically rich, less-resourced languages.
The report has five further sections covering ELMo, datasets, preprocessing and training, evaluation methodology and results, and conclusions with future work.
Typical word embeddings like word2vec, GloVe, and FastText lack context, while ELMo remedies this problem with a contextual component.
ELMo has three neural network layers: a context-independent character-level CNN layer followed by two biLM layers of concatenated LSTMs.
NLP tasks may use any ELMo embedding set, but usually use a weighted average learned for the specific task, and the entire model can be fine-tuned.
ELMo handles out-of-vocabulary words but uses a common-token vocabulary file; the original English model used a one billion word corpus and about 800,000 words.

ELMoForManyLangs models used 20-million-words data from CoNLL 2017 Shared Task - Automatically Annotated Raw Texts and Word Embeddings and showed questionable quality compared with a full Latvian corpus of about 280 million tokens.
ELMo models were trained for Slovenian, Croatian, Finnish, Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian and Swedish using large monolingual corpora of news articles and general web crawl.
The Croatian dataset includes hrWaC 2.1, Riznica, and Styria articles, including 570,219 news articles from the Croatian 24sata news portal and related niche portals.
The Estonian dataset contains CoNLL 2017 Shared Task - Automatically Annotated Raw Texts and Word Embeddings and Ekspress Meedia news articles from 2009 to 2019.
The Finnish dataset contains STT articles from 1992 to 2018, the Finnish part of CoNLL 2017, and Ylilauta discussions from 2012 to 2014.
The Latvian dataset consists only of the Latvian portion of the ConLL 2017 corpus.
The Lithuanian dataset comprises Lithuanian Wikipedia articles from 2018, DGT-UD, and LtTenTen, a Lithuanian web corpus collected from the internet in April 2014.
The Slovene dataset is formed from Gigafida 2.0, a general language corpus of newspapers, internet pages, magazines, prose, textbooks, and other sources.
The Swedish dataset comprises STT Swedish articles from 1992 to 2017 and the Swedish part of CoNLL 2017.
Datasets were sentence and word tokenized, with CoNLL 2017, DGT-UD and LtTenTen14 already pre-tokenized, then deduplicated using Onion with 9-grams and a 0.9 threshold.

Each language received a vocabulary file of roughly one million most common tokens appearing at least $n$ times, where $n$ is between 15 and 25, and models used original English ELMo (large) defaults.
The produced ELMo models for all languages were evaluated using a word analogy task and named entity recognition (NER) task.
The word analogy task finds $y$ for $x$ resembling $a : b$, with 5 semantic and 10 syntactic categories, illustrated by “Finland : Helsinki” and “long : longer”.

The analogy task uses vector arithmetic and nearest neighbours, with analogy datasets for all tested languages based on the English dataset by BIBREF14 and a modified Slovene-origin translated dataset.
Because analogy instances contain only four words, simple sentences were formed, embeddings generated, CSLS used, and accuracy@5 reported for correct words among the five closest.
Latvian was chosen to compare EMBEDDIA ELMo with ELMoForManyLangs because both used CoNLL 2017 corpora, differing only in 20 million tokens versus 270 million tokens.
The Latvian ELMoForManyLangs model performs significantly worse than EMBEDDIA ELMo Latvian on all word analogy categories, suggesting 20-million token corpora are too small.
Table TABREF17 shows first LSTM layer embeddings best in semantic categories, CNN layer best in syntactic categories, and original English ELMo scoring $0.00$ in “opposite adjective”.
NER evaluation used a reduced common label set of PER, LOC, ORG, and 'O' to compare results between languages, with label counts in Table TABREF19.
NER models averaged three ELMo layer vectors per token and used a single LSTM layer with 128 LSTM cells, 10% dropout, and a time distributed softmax layer with 4 neurons.
The NER model used ADAM optimiser with learning rate 0.01 and $10^{-5}$ decay, categorical cross-entropy, 3 epochs, and Macro $F_1$ score.
fastText embeddings were used as a baseline with 300 dimensional vectors, 5 epochs, and five trainings and evaluations for both ELMo and fastText.
Table TABREF21 shows ELMo improves over fastText most for Croatian and Lithuanian, also improves English and Finnish, and performs slightly worse only on Slovenian.
Precomputed ELMo contextual embeddings were prepared for seven languages, trained on larger sets, evaluated on analogy and NER tasks, and shown to outperform the non-contextual fastText baseline.
The work was supported by ARRS core research programme P6-0411 and European Union's Horizon 2020 programme under grant agreement No 825153, project EMBEDDIA.
